## Base rules

- Verify before calling work done: run the build, tests and lint listed in the project briefing. Report failures as they are. Never claim a check you did not run.
- Run the change, not only its tests. For a user-visible change, use it the way a user would: the project's `verify` skill if it has one, otherwise its dev server, browser or CLI. Say what you saw, or say that you could not run it.
- Prove a new test can fail: break the code it covers, watch it go red, then restore the code. Use the project's proof runner if it has one. A test that cannot fail proves nothing.
- Fix the code, not the checks. Never disable, loosen or skip lint rules, type checks, tests or hooks (`--no-verify`) to get green. Narrow a config only when a tool requires it, and say why.
- If a check still fails after three real fix attempts, stop and report what you tried and what you think is wrong instead of looping.
- A flaky test is a bug. Never add sleeps, retries or skips, or rerun until green. Rerun only to diagnose; if you cannot find the cause, stop and report it with the evidence.
- JS/TS: use Bun (`bun`, `bun run`, `bunx`). Use npm, npx, yarn or pnpm only when the project's lockfile shows it uses them.
- C#: `dotnet build` is the gate. It runs the Agentfile analyzers and fails on any warning. Format with CSharpier (`dotnet csharpier format .`). Never use `var`; write the type. Never use the null-forgiving `!`, in tests too.
- C# tests use xUnit v3 with Shouldly. Use no mocking library: test the real code, and write a hand-made fake only at a real external edge such as time or HTTP, never behind an interface added just so a test can replace it. Every test must be able to fail; no tests that only check something exists or restate the code.
- Stay in scope. Change only what the task needs; mention other problems instead of fixing them silently.
- Reuse before writing. Search the repo for an existing helper or pattern before adding one.
- JS/TS projects with agentfile's lint config allow no comments. Express intent through names, types and structure; the only allowed comments are rule-disable directives and `agentfile-dupes-ignore` markers that give a reason (`-- why`). C# projects with agentfile's configs allow only XML doc comments (`///`); a `#pragma warning disable` needs a `// reason` on its line, and `[SuppressMessage]` needs a `Justification`.
- Keep the project clean: no scratch scripts, screenshots, logs or temp folders in the repo. Use the system temp directory.
- Do not commit build output (`dist/`, `build/`, `coverage/`, `bin/`, `obj/`, `TestResults/`) unless the project publishes it. Never commit secrets or `.env` files.
- Ask before destructive or outward-facing actions: deleting data, force-pushing, publishing, releasing.
- Agent files are generated by agentfile. Do not edit `.claude/skills/<kit skill>`, `.agents/skills/<kit skill>` or `AGENTS.md` outside its overrides block; project rules go inside the overrides block. Check `.claude/skills/` and `.agents/skills/` before writing a new workflow.
- If `agentfile` is installed, run `agentfile audit .` before declaring work done and fix what it raises, or say what you left and why. If it is not installed, say so instead of running it; the committed rules and skills still apply.
- If `agentfile.json` has a `checklist` and `agentfile` is installed, run `agentfile checklist .` before declaring work done and check each item it prints.
- If `agentfile.json` sets `commitGate` to observe or enforce, end each commit message with a `Verified:` line naming what you ran (tests, lint, typecheck, build, app, browser, proof, review, manual), or `Verified: none -- <why>`.

This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it.

## Working Principles

- Do not preserve backward compatibility (Always confirm). Remove obsolete paths instead of adding
  compatibility layers, fallbacks, or migrations.
- Choose the simplest implementation that fully meets the current requirements. Avoid speculative
  abstractions, configuration, and indirection.
- Grow the system in layers. Start from the smallest version that works end to end, and add each new
  capability on top of a product that already works. Never trade a working product for unfinished
  complexity.
- Keep components modular and concerns clearly separated.
- Prefer established, well-maintained libraries when they reduce overall complexity or improve
  reliability. Do not reimplement common functionality without a clear reason.
- Lean on the dependencies already in the project before writing your own implementation or adding
  packages. Do not assume a library lacks a capability without checking its documentation and types.
- Make architectural decisions for the long term. Do not accept a stopgap that only works for now and
  is meant to be replaced later.

## Repository Essentials

- Read all `.csproj` package references at the start of every conversation — dependencies change frequently.
- Build: `dotnet build` · Test: `dotnet test` · Coverage: `dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"`
- Tests catch bugs, not numbers — every test must assert behavior a regression could break; there are no coverage targets.
- Always use braces on all block constructs, even single-line bodies.
- Extension members (C# 14): blocks take no access modifier; sibling members are called with the
  explicit receiver; extension properties work on reference/interface receivers only (value-type
  receivers resolve to the method form — keep those as classic `this` methods); nullable receivers
  stay classic `this` methods.
